Lessons.Title: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 G5 U04:L11 Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity compares multiple valid decompositions of WHOLE-NUMBER DIVISION by a two-digit divisor, including sets of quotient chunks and metacognitive choice of a useful first multiple. The sum of selected partial QUOTIENTS must equal the full quotient, and corresponding products must partition the ORIGINAL dividend.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder Ways to Record: source 364÷13=28 is recorded through Clare/Jada different decompositions. Source examples include 13×10=130,13×20=260,13×5=65,13×3=39; 260+65+39=364 and partial quotients 20+5+3=28. A source figure may also present 130+130+65+39=364. Teacher reviews actual partial-quotient records rather than assuming a unique order.

Activity 1 Division Expressions: original source card activity targets 308÷14=22. Learners select an actual set of expressions whose partial QUOTIENTS add to 22 and whose dividend chunks sum to 308, leaving zero. Actual original option card deck is not independently verified; do not claim invented card expressions are publisher originals. Correct independent example 14×20=280 then14×2=28.

Activity 2 Choose Your Own Partial Quotients: source exercises 360÷15=24 (e.g. 300÷15=20 and60÷15=4), 945÷45=21 (900÷45=20 and45÷45=1) and 992÷31=32 (e.g. 31×30=930 and62÷31=2). Teacher asks children to choose a first useful partial quotient, compare possible start values and revise when needed. Some source card expressions such as 341÷31=11 are helper chunks, not full 992÷31.

Exact selected Practice covers verified source quotients and helper chunks only. Teacher reviews card selection, original source diagram interpretation, complete remainder zero and partner explanations. Edulytiks independent teacher Cool-down 672÷24=28 does not recreate the publisher gated original.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient is a counted group
KeyConcepts.Definition: A partial quotient counts a portion of the final equal-sized groups.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If 320÷16=20, then 20 full groups of 16 consume 320.

KeyConcepts.Title: Several correct decompositions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different sums of divisor-multiples can reconstruct the same dividend.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose an efficient chunk
KeyConcepts.Definition: A larger convenient multiple can reduce the number of subtraction steps without changing the quotient.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source 364÷13 partial quotients
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare two ways to divide 364 by 13 with convenient chunks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Sum valid multiples of divisor and their quotient contributions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original 308÷14 card-sum target
WorkedExamples.Question: Choose chunks that make 308÷14 with an exact zero remainder.
WorkedExamples.Method: Source task accepts different partial-quotient sets, not a single invented card match.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source three student-selected division targets
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 360÷15,945÷45,992÷31.
WorkedExamples.Method: Start with convenient tens of divisor then finish remaining groups.

WorkedExamples.Question: Show two legal partial-quotient methods for 352÷16.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.
Steps: Method two: remove 160 twice (two groups of ten) then32.
Add partial quotients in each method.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Choose large easy chunks
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 832÷26 starting with 30 groups.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Reject an incomplete set
WorkedExamples.Question: A student records only 20 groups of 16 for 352÷16. Explain the missing work.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the only correct route is the shortest list
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Valid smaller partial chunks are acceptable if they cover the dividend exactly.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify every group count and total; discuss efficiency as a separate criterion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Sum partial quotients without checking subtracted multiples
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A correct-looking sum can mask omitted or duplicated dividend pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply each selected partial quotient by the divisor and sum to the original dividend.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace source 308÷14 and 360÷15,945÷45,992÷31 with invented 352÷16 and 832÷26
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original printed lesson uses named different quotient targets and specific helper expressions, and expects student source card selection.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore all source totals and verified helpers; keep alternative division examples explicitly optional.

SummaryPoints: Source warmup 364÷13=28 using different valid source partial-quotient representations.
Source Activity1 target 308÷14=22, with full original card deck not independently certified.
Original partner discussions require full dividend accounting and a remainder of zero.
Selected numeric quotient cases are supplemental; teacher scores actual source diagrams and choices.

Lessons.Title: An Algorithm Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret and use a written PARTIAL QUOTIENTS algorithm for division by a two-digit divisor. Connect each subtraction of a convenient divisor multiple to the number of whole groups removed, then keep track of the remaining quantity and total quotient.

Warm-up: inspect an incomplete first-party partial-quotient layout for 588÷21, displaying dividend 588 and subtracting 420. Ask what the 420 represents (20 groups of 21) and what remains, rather than guessing the final answer from surface features.

Activity 1 — label each line: calculate 588÷21 by subtracting 420=20×21, leaving168; subtract 126=6×21, leaving42; subtract42=2×21, leaving0. Sum partial quotients 20+6+2=28. Explain the roles of multiplication and subtraction at every step.

Activity 2 — use less scaffolding: for 768÷24, subtract 720=30×24 leaving48, then subtract 48=2×24 leaving0. Alternatively subtract 480 then 240 then48 for partial quotients 20,10,2. Compare the remaining values and show the same 32 groups.

Academic boundary: source asks learners to make sense of the actual written algorithm, what every number means and how partial quotients are recorded, including self-explanation. The final 28/32 number alone cannot grade whether the learner has represented the algorithm properly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient recording
KeyConcepts.Definition: A division algorithm may repeatedly subtract whole multiples of a divisor while recording group counts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Remaining dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: The remainder at each step is how much of the original dividend is not yet allocated.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Continue subtracting valid divisor multiples until remaining is below divisor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplication verifies division
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quotient q with remainder r must satisfy divisor×q+r=dividend and 0≤r<divisor.
KeyConcepts.Example: A remainder of 42 with divisor 21 is not final.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read every subtraction row
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 588÷21 by three partial quotients.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose a larger chunk
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 768÷24 using two steps.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use smaller chunks instead
WorkedExamples.Question: Show 768÷24 with 20,10,2 groups.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract the quotient count rather than the product
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Subtracting '20' directly is incorrect when 20 groups each have 21 items.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute 20×21=420 and subtract that from the dividend.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Stop with a remainder greater than or equal to divisor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Another full group can still be removed if enough quantity remains.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Continue until the final whole-number remainder is smaller than the divisor.

SummaryPoints: A partial-quotients algorithm combines subtraction, multiplication and addition.
Every subtracted product represents a specific number of equal groups.
Explanation of each recorded algorithm step is teacher-reviewed.

Source: IM K–5 Math Grade 5 (first edition 2021), Unit 4 Lesson 12, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-4/lesson-12/lesson.html. Original Edulytiks worked math and tables; public source HTML inspected, source student PDF and protected response/Cool-down not independently reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Divide Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: select reasonable PARTIAL QUOTIENTS for increasingly unfamiliar 3- and 4-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, estimate BEFORE calculating, and compare different student approaches. Source lesson specifically asks learners to explain why an efficient first multiple is chosen.
Warm-up: compare several 11-times whole numbers: 110÷10=11,121÷11=11,132÷12=11. Explain how using a quotient benchmark can guide a division method without reproducing a fixed diagram.

Activity 1 — two partners, different choices: Student A solves 672÷28 by subtracting560=20×28, leaving112, then112=4×28; Student B subtracts 280 twice then112, using partial quotients 10+10+4. Both yield24. Discuss why the less efficient route is still correct and what information the initial estimate gives.

Activity 2 — estimate and solve: for 988÷38, estimate near 1000÷40≈25. Subtract760=20×38 leaving228, then228=6×38, so exact quotient26. Check that the 26 result is close to benchmark25. If a learner chooses 10+10+6 instead, demonstrate the same final dividend accounting.

Teacher boundary: the source requires comparing different algorithms, strategy revision and an estimate, not one preferred exact layout. Numeric checking supports correct division, but learner justification, estimating and peer comparison require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate guides division
KeyConcepts.Definition: A convenient nearby dividend/divisor can give a quotient magnitude before detailed partial-quotient steps.

KeyConcepts.Title: Many equivalent partial-quotient plans
KeyConcepts.Definition: Valid plans can subtract different convenient divisor-multiples while giving same final count.

KeyConcepts.Title: Complete exact verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: The sum of partial group counts plus any final remainder must reconstruct dividend.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two strategies
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 672÷28 with both a 20+4 and 10+10+4 plan.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.
Steps: Add the partial quotients and compare the explanations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate quotient size
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 988÷38 using friendly nearby numbers.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.
Steps: Describe the expected result as around25.
WorkedExamples.Check: The exact quotient26 is close, not necessarily equal to the estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute from estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: Finish 988÷38 exactly.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a quotient estimate as an exact answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rounding factors can shift the quotient.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use estimates to guide partial quotients, then verify exact multiplication.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A different combination of legal partial quotients can be mathematically equivalent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check whether all subtracted divisor-multiples account for the dividend.

SummaryPoints: Estimate the quotient before selecting partial-quotient group counts.
Different valid partial-quotient decompositions can be compared without penalizing correct alternatives.
Partner explanation and strategic selection require teacher review.

Source: IM K–5 Math Grade 5 (first edition 2021), Unit 4 Lesson 13, https://im.kendallhunt.com/k5/teachers/grade-5/unit-4/lesson-13/lesson.html. Original Edulytiks worked math and tables; public source HTML inspected, source student PDF and protected response/Cool-down not independently reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Practice an Algorithm Using Partial Quotients
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: find and explain ERRORS in partial-quotient division and then handle larger four-digit dividends with strategic HUNDREDS-sized quotient chunks. The 2021 lesson expects diagnosing wrong multiplication or subtraction, not just finding correct results elsewhere.

Warm-up: compare partial-quotient methods with many small multiples and fewer large multiples; consider different valid Which One Doesn't Belong reasons. A short method need not be less understandable than a longer method, and multiple correct methods are allowed.

Activity 1 — original error analysis: a student divides 832 by26 by subtracting a claimed 30×26=750, then uses the remaining82 to obtain three more groups. Identify the incorrectly multiplied chunk (30×26 is780, not750) and explain the correct remaining 52 and final quotient32. In another attempt subtract 780 correctly but mistakenly record 832−780=62; correct to52. Require students to explain each arithmetic error's consequence.

Activity 2 — four-digit division with large chunks: for 8415÷33, start with 200 groups (6600), leaving1815; subtract50 groups (1650), leaving165; subtract5 groups (165), leaving0. Sum200+50+5=255. For 7344÷24, start300 groups (7200), leave144, then6 groups (144), total306. Confirm divisor×quotient=dividend.

Teacher boundary: source critiques errors, compares partial quotient choices and requires large multi-digit calculation with interpretation. Checking only 255 or306 cannot certify correct algorithm debugging or partner discussion. Publisher long-division pictures and protected response are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Error diagnosis in partial quotients
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mistaken product or subtraction changes the remaining amount and can create false quotient claims.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use hundreds-sized chunks
KeyConcepts.Definition: For four-digit dividends, subtracting 100 or200 divisor groups at once may be more efficient.
KeyConcepts.Example: The remaining1815 is still divisible by33.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent multiplication check
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid exact quotient must reproduce the dividend when multiplied by the divisor.
KeyConcepts.Example: The final remainder must also be below the divisor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a multiplication error
WorkedExamples.Question: A partial-quotient step says30×26=750 while dividing832 by26. What is wrong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 32; the stated 750 partial product is incorrect.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a subtraction error
WorkedExamples.Question: The same problem records832−780=62. Correct it.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four-digit partial quotient
WorkedExamples.Question: Find8415÷33 using large chunks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Another four-digit quotient
WorkedExamples.Question: Find7344÷24.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use first-party partial-quotient reasoning with independently checked multiplication and subtraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept a plausible rounded partial product as exact
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Partial quotients require exact divisor multiples and exact subtraction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check each chosen chunk with multiplication before removing it.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use only tens-sized chunks for every large dividend
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Small chunks may work but cause avoidable repetitive work for four-digit dividends.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Consider a 100- or 200-group chunk and verify it does not exceed the remainder.

SummaryPoints: Error checking must distinguish incorrect multiplication from incorrect subtraction.
Hundreds-sized partial quotients can efficiently divide four-digit numbers.
Teacher reviews diagnosis, correction and explanation; exact numbers are supporting checks.
